metadata.title: Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes

extraction_notes.note: All lemmas and theorems are classical textbook results (Kummer's argument), the introduction says the text 'uses' Samuel, Marcus and Washington; marked origin external although several are re-proved here, their proofs are origin paper.

Theorem 18 is a list of five facts proved item by item and used item by item (parts 4 and 5 in the proof of Theorem 19, part 3 in part 5); each item is a nested claim and each proof item a labelled step.
Blueprint: these results are stated without proof; the dependencies LP12->LP13, LP7->LP8, TP4->TP5 are inferred from the standard arguments, not stated.

metadata.extraction_comment: References written 'Proposition \ref{...}' point at lemma environments; the finishing step resolves them by label.

nodes.name: Trace and norm via embeddings
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field, $\alpha \in K$ and let $\sigma_i$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Then \[\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha) =\sum_i \sigma_i(\alpha) \qquad N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\prod_i \sigma_i(\alpha) \]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ be a number field, $\alpha \in K$ and let $\sigma_i$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$
conclusions: \[\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha) =\sum_i \sigma_i(\alpha) \qquad N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=\prod_i \sigma_i(\alpha) \]
nodes.statement_short: Trace and norm of $\alpha$ are the sum and product of its images under the embeddings of $K$.
nodes.label: lemma: alt definition of norm and trace

nodes.name: Discriminant via embeddings
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field with basis $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$. Now let $M$ be the matrix \[\left (\begin{matrix} \sigma_1(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_1(b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \sigma_n(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_n(b_n) \end{matrix} \right ).\] Then \[\Delta(B)=\det(M)^2.\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ be a number field with basis $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ and let $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n$ be the embeddings of $K$ into $\mathbb{C}$
let $M$ be the matrix \[\left (\begin{matrix} \sigma_1(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_1(b_n)\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \sigma_n(b_1) &\cdots& \sigma_n(b_n) \end{matrix} \right ).\]
conclusions: \[\Delta(B)=\det(M)^2.\]
nodes.statement_short: The discriminant of a basis is the square of the determinant of the matrix of its embeddings.
nodes.label: lemma: disc via embs

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2 (discriminant via embeddings)
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lemma: alt definition of norm and trace} we know that $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(b_i b_j)= \sum_k \sigma_k(b_i)\sigma_k(b_j)$ which is the same as the $(i,j)$ entry of $M^t M$. Therefore \[\det(T_B)=\det(M^t M)=\det(M)^2.\]
nodes.statement_short: Trace matrix equals $M^tM$ by Lemma 1, take determinants.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a power basis
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$ for some $\alpha \in K$. Then \[\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j} (\sigma_i(\alpha)-\sigma_j(\alpha))^2\] where $\sigma_i$ are the embeddings of $K $ into $\mathbb{C}$. Here $\Delta(B)$ denotes the discriminant.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$ for some $\alpha \in K$
conclusions: \[\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j} (\sigma_i(\alpha)-\sigma_j(\alpha))^2\] where $\sigma_i$ are the embeddings of $K $ into $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant of the power basis of $\alpha$ is the squared Vandermonde product of its conjugates.
nodes.label: lemma: disc of prim elt basis

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3 (discriminant of a power basis)
nodes.statement: First we recall a classical linear algebra result relating to the Vandermonde matrix, which states that \[\det \left (\begin{matrix} 1 & x_1& x_1^2&\cdots&x_1^{n-1} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ 1 & x_n& x_n^2&\cdots&x_n^{n-1} \end{matrix} \right ) =\prod_{i<j} (x_i-x_j).\] Combining this with Proposition \ref{lemma: disc via embs} gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Vandermonde determinant combined with Lemma 2.

nodes.name: Derivative of an irreducible polynomial at a root
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a monic irreducible polynomial over a number field $K$ and let $\alpha$ be one of its roots in $\mathbb{C}$. Then \[f'(\alpha)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (\alpha-\beta), \] where the product is over the roots of $f$ different from $\alpha$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $f$ be a monic irreducible polynomial over a number field $K$
$\alpha$ be one of its roots in $\mathbb{C}$
conclusions: \[f'(\alpha)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (\alpha-\beta), \] where the product is over the roots of $f$ different from $\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: $f'(\alpha)$ is the product of $\alpha-\beta$ over the other roots $\beta$ of $f$.
nodes.label: lemma: diff of irr pol

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: We first write $f(x)=(x-\alpha)g(x)$ which we can do (over $\mathbb{C}$) as $\alpha$ is a root of $f$, where now $g(x)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (x-\beta)$. Differentiating we get \[f'(x)=g(x)+(x-\alpha)g'(x).\] If we now evaluate at $\alpha$ we get the result.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f=(x-\alpha)g$, differentiate by the product rule and evaluate at $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Factor out the root
nodes.statement: We first write $f(x)=(x-\alpha)g(x)$ which we can do (over $\mathbb{C}$) as $\alpha$ is a root of $f$, where now $g(x)=\prod_{\beta \neq \alpha} (x-\beta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $f(x)=(x-\alpha)g(x)$.

nodes.name: Differentiate
nodes.statement: Differentiating we get \[f'(x)=g(x)+(x-\alpha)g'(x).\]
nodes.statement_short: Product rule for $f'$.

nodes.name: Evaluate at the root
nodes.statement: If we now evaluate at $\alpha$ we get the result.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate at $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Discriminant of a number field in terms of the norm
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be a number field with $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ and let $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$. Then \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))\] where $m_\alpha'$ is the derivative of $m_\alpha(x)$ (which we recall denotes the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$).
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$ be a number field with $n=[K:\mathbb{Q}]$
let $B=\{1,\alpha,\alpha^2,\dots,\alpha^{n-1}\}$
conclusions: \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))\] where $m_\alpha'$ is the derivative of $m_\alpha(x)$ (which we recall denotes the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$).
nodes.statement_short: Power-basis discriminant equals $\pm$ the norm of $m_\alpha'(\alpha)$, sign $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$.
nodes.label: lemma: num field disc in terms of norm

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lemma: disc of prim elt basis} we have $\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ where $\alpha_k:=\sigma_k(\alpha)$. Next, we note that the number of terms in this product is $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. So if we write each term as $(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=-(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)(\alpha_j-\alpha_i)$ we get \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j). \] Now, by lemmama \ref{lemma: diff of irr pol} and Proposition \ref{lemma: alt definition of norm and trace} we see that \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))=\prod_{i=1}^n m_\alpha'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j),\] which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the Vandermonde product of Lemma 3 with a sign, then identify it with the norm of $m_\alpha'(\alpha)$ via Lemmas 4 and 1.

nodes.name: Apply the power-basis formula
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{lemma: disc of prim elt basis} we have $\Delta(B)=\prod_{i < j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$ where $\alpha_k:=\sigma_k(\alpha)$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 gives the Vandermonde product.

nodes.name: Extract the sign
nodes.statement: Next, we note that the number of terms in this product is $1+2+\cdots+(n-1)=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$. So if we write each term as $(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=-(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)(\alpha_j-\alpha_i)$ we get \[\Delta(B)=(-1)^{\frac{n(n-1)}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j). \]
nodes.statement_short: Count the $n(n-1)/2$ factors and pull out the sign.

nodes.name: Identify with the norm
nodes.statement: Now, by lemmama \ref{lemma: diff of irr pol} and Proposition \ref{lemma: alt definition of norm and trace} we see that \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(m_\alpha'(\alpha))=\prod_{i=1}^n m_\alpha'(\alpha_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n \prod_{i \neq j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j),\] which gives the result.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 4 and 1 identify the product with $N(m_\alpha'(\alpha))$.

nodes.name: Discriminant under change of basis
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B,B'$ bases for $K/\mathbb{Q}$. If $P$ denotes the change of basis matrix, then \[\Delta(B)=\det(P)^2 \Delta(B').\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and $B,B'$ bases for $K/\mathbb{Q}$
$P$ denotes the change of basis matrix
conclusions: \[\Delta(B)=\det(P)^2 \Delta(B').\]
nodes.label: lemma: disc change of basis

nodes.name: Norm and trace of an algebraic integer are integers
nodes.statement: If $K$ is a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ and $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ are both in $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ is a number field and $\alpha \in \mathcal{O}_K$
conclusions: $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ and $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ are both in $\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.label: lemma: norm trace of alg int is int

nodes.name: Discriminant of algebraic integers is an integer
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be elements in $\mathcal{O}_K$, then $\Delta(B) \in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be elements in $\mathcal{O}_K$
conclusions: $\Delta(B) \in \mathbb{Z}$
nodes.label: lemma: int basis int disc

nodes.name: Non-integral basis criterion via discriminant
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a basis for $K/\mathbb{Q}$ consisting of algebraic integers. If $B$ is not an integral basis then there exists an algebraic integer of the form \[\alpha=\frac{x_1b_1+\cdots+x_nb_n}{p}\] where $p$ is a prime and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ with not all $x_i$ zero. Moreover, if $x_i \neq 0$ and we let $B'$ be the basis obtained by replacing $b_i$ with $\alpha$, then \[\Delta(B')= \frac{x_i^2}{p^2} \Delta(B).\] In particular $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K$ be a number field and $B=\{b_1,\dots,b_n\}$ be a basis for $K/\mathbb{Q}$ consisting of algebraic integers
$B$ is not an integral basis
$x_i \neq 0$ and we let $B'$ be the basis obtained by replacing $b_i$ with $\alpha$
conclusions: there exists an algebraic integer of the form \[\alpha=\frac{x_1b_1+\cdots+x_nb_n}{p}\] where $p$ is a prime and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ with not all $x_i$ zero
\[\Delta(B')= \frac{x_i^2}{p^2} \Delta(B).\]
$p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$

assumptions: $B$ is not an integral basis
conclusions: there exists an algebraic integer of the form \[\alpha=\frac{x_1b_1+\cdots+x_nb_n}{p}\] where $p$ is a prime and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ with not all $x_i$ zero

assumptions: $x_i \neq 0$ and we let $B'$ be the basis obtained by replacing $b_i$ with $\alpha$
conclusions: \[\Delta(B')= \frac{x_i^2}{p^2} \Delta(B).\]
$p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$

nodes.statement_short: If an algebraic-integer basis is not integral, some $(\sum x_ib_i)/p$ is integral, swapping it in divides the discriminant by $p^2/x_i^2$, so $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$.
nodes.label: lemma: disc int basis

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: If $B$ is not an integral basis then we can find some element $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with not all the $y_i$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. So, let $N$ be the least common multiple of the denominators of the $y_i$ (meaning $Ny_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$). Now, let $p$ be a prime factor of $N$. If we now consider $(N/p)\phi$ then all of the coefficients of $b_i$ are in $\frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$ (so they have denominator $1$ or $p$.) and at least one of them has denominator $p$ (since not all the $y_i$ where in $\mathbb{Z}$). So by relabelling, wlog we can assume \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with $y_i \in \frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$ Now look at \[\psi:=\lfloor y_1 \rfloor b_1+\cdots+\lfloor y_n \rfloor b_n\] (here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the integer part of $x$). The both $\psi$ and $\phi$ are algebraic integers (as the $b_i$ are algebraic integers). Therefore, so is $\theta=\phi-\psi$. By construction, $\theta$ has coefficients of the for $\frac{x_i}{p}:=y_i-\lfloor y_i \rfloor$ where $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and not all the $x_i$ are zero (since, again, not all the $y_i$ were in $\mathbb{Z}$). This gives the first part of the lemma. Now, assume $x_i \neq 0$, then let us replace $b_i \in B$ with $\theta$ to get a new basis $B'$ which again consists of algebraic integers. Next, we note that the change of basis matrix from $B$ to $B'$ is \[ \left( \begin{matrix} 1&0&\cdots& \frac{x_1}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ 0&1&\cdots& \frac{x_2}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ \vdots& \vdots&&\vdots&&\vdots \\ 0&0&\cdots& \frac{x_n}{p}& \cdots &1 \\ \end{matrix} \right) \](here the column of $x_j/p$'s is in the $i$-th column). This matrix has determinant $\frac{x_i}{p}.$ Therefore, by Proposition \ref{lemma: disc change of basis} we see that $\Delta(B')=\frac{x_i^2}{p^2}\Delta(B)$. But both $\Delta(B),\Delta(B')$ are in $\mathbb{Z}$ by Proposition \ref{lemma: int basis int disc}, therefore $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$ giving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Construct a new integral element with coefficients in $\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$ by clearing denominators and subtracting integer parts. Swapping it into the basis scales the discriminant by $x_i^2/p^2$ (Lemma 6), and integrality (Lemma 8) forces $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$.

nodes.name: Non-integral element and prime denominator
nodes.statement: If $B$ is not an integral basis then we can find some element $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ such that \[\phi=y_1b_1+\dots y_nb_n\] with not all the $y_i$ in $\mathbb{Z}$. So, let $N$ be the least common multiple of the denominators of the $y_i$ (meaning $Ny_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for all $i$). Now, let $p$ be a prime factor of $N$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $\phi$ with non-integer coordinates, $N$ the lcm of denominators and $p\mid N$.

nodes.name: Reduce to denominators p
nodes.statement: If we now consider $(N/p)\phi$ then all of the coefficients of $b_i$ are in $\frac{1}{p} \mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $N/p$ so coefficients lie in $\frac1p\mathbb{Z}$; wlog.

nodes.name: Subtract integer parts
nodes.statement: Now look at \[\psi:=\lfloor y_1 \rfloor b_1+\cdots+\lfloor y_n \rfloor b_n\] (here $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the integer part of $x$). The both $\psi$ and $\phi$ are algebraic integers (as the $b_i$ are algebraic integers). Therefore, so is $\theta=\phi-\psi$. By construction, $\theta$ has coefficients of the for $\frac{x_i}{p}:=y_i-\lfloor y_i \rfloor$ where $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}$ and not all the $x_i$ are zero (since, again, not all the $y_i$ were in $\mathbb{Z}$). This gives the first part of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: $\theta=\phi-\psi$ is integral with coefficients $x_i/p$, giving the first part.

nodes.name: Swap into the basis
nodes.statement: Now, assume $x_i \neq 0$, then let us replace $b_i \in B$ with $\theta$ to get a new basis $B'$ which again consists of algebraic integers. Next, we note that the change of basis matrix from $B$ to $B'$ is \[ \left( \begin{matrix} 1&0&\cdots& \frac{x_1}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ 0&1&\cdots& \frac{x_2}{p}& \cdots &0 \\ \vdots& \vdots&&\vdots&&\vdots \\ 0&0&\cdots& \frac{x_n}{p}& \cdots &1 \\ \end{matrix} \right) \](here the column of $x_j/p$'s is in the $i$-th column).
nodes.statement_short: Replace $b_i$ by $\theta$ and write the change-of-basis matrix.

nodes.name: Compare discriminants
nodes.statement: This matrix has determinant $\frac{x_i}{p}.$ Therefore, by Proposition \ref{lemma: disc change of basis} we see that $\Delta(B')=\frac{x_i^2}{p^2}\Delta(B)$. But both $\Delta(B),\Delta(B')$ are in $\mathbb{Z}$ by Proposition \ref{lemma: int basis int disc}, therefore $p^2 \mid \Delta(B)$ giving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6 scales $\Delta$ by $x_i^2/p^2$; Lemma 8 gives $p^2\mid\Delta(B)$.

nodes.name: Eisenstein criterion and algebraic integers
nodes.statement: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$and $\alpha$ be an algebraic integer such that $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisensteins Criterion for a prime $p$. Then none of the elements \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_0+x_1\alpha+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1})\] is an algebraic integer, where $n=\deg(m_\alpha)$ and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}.$
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $K=\mathbb{Q}(\alpha)$and $\alpha$ be an algebraic integer such that $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisensteins Criterion for a prime $p$
$n=\deg(m_\alpha)$ and $x_i \in \{0,\dots,p-1\}.$
conclusions: none of the elements \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_0+x_1\alpha+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1})\] is an algebraic integer
nodes.statement_short: If $m_\alpha$ is $p$-Eisenstein, no $\frac1p\sum x_i\alpha^i$ with $0\le x_i<p$ (not all zero) is an algebraic integer.
nodes.label: lemma: eis crit and alg ints

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: We will only prove the case when $m_\alpha$ is Eisenstein, since the proof of the more general case is identical. Suppose for contradiction that $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and let $x_d$ be the first non-zero coefficient, so \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d+x_{d+1}\alpha^{d+1}+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] Now, rewrite this as $\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d +\alpha^{d+1}\beta)$ for some $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$. Next, multiply through by $\alpha^{n-1-d}$, then we have \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\frac{\alpha^n\beta}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] Now, since $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisenstein at $p$, we see that $\alpha^n=pf(\alpha)$ for some $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and therefore the above gives us that \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\beta f(\alpha) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] and thus \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] Lets now calculate the norm of this: \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{n-1}}{p^n}.\] By Eisenstein the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is divisible by $p$ but not $p^2$, so since the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ we see that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=p a$ where $p \nmid a$. Therefore we have \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n p^{n-1}a^{n-1}}{p^n}= \frac{x_d^n a^{n-1}}{p}.\] But this cant be in $\mathbb{Z}$ since $p$ doesn't divide $x_d$ or $a$, and this gives us a contradiction since Proposition \ref{lemma: norm trace of alg int is int} says that the norm of an algebraic integer must be an integer. So $\phi$ couldn't have been an algebraic integer.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: isolate the leading term, use $\alpha^n\in p\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ to get $x_d\alpha^{n-1}/p$ integral. Its norm $x_d^na^{n-1}/p$ is not an integer, contradicting Lemma 7.

nodes.name: Restrict to the Eisenstein case
nodes.statement: We will only prove the case when $m_\alpha$ is Eisenstein, since the proof of the more general case is identical.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $m_\alpha$ Eisenstein.

nodes.name: Assume an integral element
nodes.statement: Suppose for contradiction that $\phi \in \mathcal{O}_K$ and let $x_d$ be the first non-zero coefficient, so \[\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d+x_{d+1}\alpha^{d+1}+\cdots+x_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\]
nodes.statement_short: Assume $\phi$ integral, $x_d$ the first non-zero coefficient.

nodes.name: Multiply by a power of alpha
nodes.statement: Now, rewrite this as $\phi=\frac{1}{p}(x_d\alpha^d +\alpha^{d+1}\beta)$ for some $\beta \in \mathcal{O}_K$. Next, multiply through by $\alpha^{n-1-d}$, then we have \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\frac{\alpha^n\beta}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\]
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by $\alpha^{n-1-d}$.

nodes.name: Use the Eisenstein condition
nodes.statement: Now, since $m_\alpha$ satisfies Eisenstein at $p$, we see that $\alpha^n=pf(\alpha)$ for some $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ and therefore the above gives us that \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p}+\beta f(\alpha) \in \mathcal{O}_K.\] and thus \[\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \in \mathcal{O}_K.\]
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha^n=pf(\alpha)$ so $x_d\alpha^{n-1}/p$ is integral.

nodes.name: Compute the norm
nodes.statement: Lets now calculate the norm of this: \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)^{n-1}}{p^n}.\] By Eisenstein the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is divisible by $p$ but not $p^2$, so since the constant coefficient of $m_\alpha$ is $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)$ we see that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\alpha)=p a$ where $p \nmid a$. Therefore we have \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}} \left(\frac{x_d\alpha^{n-1}}{p} \right)=\frac{x_d^n p^{n-1}a^{n-1}}{p^n}= \frac{x_d^n a^{n-1}}{p}.\]
nodes.statement_short: Norm equals $x_d^na^{n-1}/p$ since $N(\alpha)=pa$.

nodes.name: Contradiction with integrality of norms
nodes.statement: But this cant be in $\mathbb{Z}$ since $p$ doesn't divide $x_d$ or $a$, and this gives us a contradiction since Proposition \ref{lemma: norm trace of alg int is int} says that the norm of an algebraic integer must be an integer. So $\phi$ couldn't have been an algebraic integer.
nodes.statement_short: Not an integer, contradicting Lemma 7.

nodes.name: Irreducibility of cyclotomic polynomials
nodes.statement: For $n$ any integer, $\Phi_n$ (the $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial) is an irreducible polynomial of degree $\varphi(n)$ (where $\varphi$ is Euler's Totient function).
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $n$ any integer
conclusions: $\Phi_n$ (the $n$-th cyclotomic polynomial) is an irreducible polynomial of degree $\varphi(n)$ (where $\varphi$ is Euler's Totient function)
nodes.label: lemma: cyclo poly

nodes.name: Ring of integers of the p-th cyclotomic field
nodes.statement: Let $\zeta_p$ be a $p$-th root of unity for $p$ an odd prime, let $\lambda_p=1-\zeta_p$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. Then $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_p]$ moreover \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_p,\dots,\lambda_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}p^{p-2}.\]
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $\zeta_p$ be a $p$-th root of unity for $p$ an odd prime, let $\lambda_p=1-\zeta_p$ and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$
conclusions: $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_p]$
\[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_p,\dots,\lambda_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}p^{p-2}.\]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12
nodes.statement: First note $[K:\mathbb{Q}]=p-1$. Since $\zeta_p=1-\lambda_p$ we at once get $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]=\mathbb{Z}[\lambda_p]$ (just do double inclusion). Next, let $\alpha_i=\sigma_i(\zeta_p)$ denote the conjugates of $\zeta_p$, which is the same as the image of $\zeta_p$ under one of the embeddings $\sigma_i: \mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p) \to \mathbb{C}$. Now by Proposition $\ref{lemma: disc of prim elt basis}$ we have \begin{align*}\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=\prod_{i < j} (\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2 &=\prod_{i < j} ((1-\alpha_i)-(1-\alpha_j))^2\\&=\Delta(\{1,\lambda_p,\dots,\lambda_p^{p-2}\})\end{align*} Now, by Proposition \ref{lemma: num field disc in terms of norm}, we have \[\Delta(\{1,\zeta_p,\cdots,\zeta_p^{p-2}\})=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )\] Since $p$ is odd $(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}$. Next, we see that \[\Phi_p'(x)=\frac{px^{p-1}(x-1)-(x^p-1)}{(x-1)^2}\] therefore \[\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-\frac{p\zeta_p^{p-1}}{\lambda_p}.\] Lastly, note that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)=1$, since this is the constant term in its minimal polynomial. Similarly, we see $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\lambda_p)=p$. Putting this all together, we get \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )=\frac{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(p)N_{K\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)^{p-1}}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(-\lambda_p)}=(-1)^{p-1}p^{p-2}=p^{p-2}\] So the last thing we need to prove is that $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. From the calculation we just did, the only prime dividing the discriminant is $p$, therefore Lemma \ref{lemma: disc int basis} tells us the only prime we need to check is $p$. But from Lemma \ref{lemma: eis crit and alg ints} we know that dividing by $p$ wont give us any new integral elements, so this must be an integral basis which give the result.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the power-basis discriminant via Lemmas 3 and 5 and $\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)$. Since only $p$ divides it, Lemmas 9 and 10 (Eisenstein) show the power basis is integral.

nodes.name: Sign and derivative of Phi_p
nodes.statement: Since $p$ is odd $(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)(p-2)}{2}}=(-1)^{\frac{(p-1)}{2}}$. Next, we see that \[\Phi_p'(x)=\frac{px^{p-1}(x-1)-(x^p-1)}{(x-1)^2}\] therefore \[\Phi_p'(\zeta_p)=-\frac{p\zeta_p^{p-1}}{\lambda_p}.\]

nodes.name: Compute the norm
nodes.statement: Lastly, note that $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)=1$, since this is the constant term in its minimal polynomial. Similarly, we see $N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\lambda_p)=p$. Putting this all together, we get \[N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(\Phi_p'(\zeta_p) )=\frac{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(p)N_{K\mathbb{Q}}(\zeta_p)^{p-1}}{N_{K/\mathbb{Q}}(-\lambda_p)}=(-1)^{p-1}p^{p-2}=p^{p-2}\]

nodes.name: Integral basis

nodes.statement: Let $p \geq 5$ be an prime number, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. Assume that we have $x,y,z \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $\gcd(xyz,p)=1$ and such that \[x^p+y^p=z^p.\] \begin{enumerate} \item We cannot have \[x \equiv y \equiv -z \pmod p\] and, therefore, without loss of generality, we may assume \[x \not \equiv y \mod p.\] \item For $i \neq j$ we can write \[(\zeta_p^i-\zeta_p^j)=u(1-\zeta_p)\] with $u$ a unit in $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. From this it follows that the ideals \[(x+y),(x+\zeta_py),(x+\zeta_p^2y),\dots,(x+\zeta_p^{p-1}y)\] are pairwise coprime. \item Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. Then $\alpha^p$ is congruent to an integer modulo $p$. \item Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. Suppose that $\alpha=a_0+a_1\zeta_p+\cdots+a_{p-1}\zeta_p^{p-1}$ with at least one $a_i=0$. Then there is an integer $n$ such that $\alpha/n \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$, then $n$ divides each $a_i$. \item Let $i \in \{1,\dots,p-1\}.$ Suppose that $x+y\zeta_p^i=u \alpha^p$ with $u \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]^\times$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$. By considering $x+y\zeta_p^i$ and its complex conjugate then there is an integer $k$ such that \[x+y\zeta_p^i-\zeta_p^{2k}x-\zeta_p^{2k-i}y \equiv 0 \pmod p.\] \end{enumerate}

It must then also divide their sum and their difference, so we must have $\mathfrak{p} | (1-\zeta_p)$ or $\mathfrak{p} | y$. But from lectures we know that since $(1-\zeta_p)$ has norm $p$ it must be a prime ideal, so $\mathfrak{p}=(1-\zeta_p)$. Now, note that $x+y \equiv x+y\zeta_+p^i \equiv 0 \mod \mathfrak{p}$. But since $x,y \in \mathbb{Z}$ this means we would have $x+y \equiv 0 \pmod p$, which implies $z^p \equiv 0 \pmod p$ which contradicts our assumptions. \item This is easy. Just use $(x+y)^p \equiv x^p + y^p \pmod p$ and that $\zeta_p$ is a $p$-th root of unity. \item Looking at $\alpha=a_0+a_1\zeta_p+\cdots+a_{p-1}\zeta_p^{p-1}$, if one of the $a_i$'s is zero and $\alpha/n \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$, then $\alpha/n=\sum_i a_i/n \zeta_p^i$. Now, as $\alpha/n \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$, pick the basis of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$ which does not contain $\zeta_p$ (which is possible as any subset of $\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-1}\}$ with $p-1$ elements forms a basis of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$.]). Then $\alpha=\sum_i b_i \zeta_p^i$ where $b_i \in \mathbb{Z}$. Therefore comparing coefficients, we get the result. \item Using lemma ef{lemma: unit lemma} we have $(x+y\zeta_p^i) = eta \zeta_p^k \alpha^p$ which is equivalent to $ eta \zeta_p^k a \pmod p$ with $a$ and integer (using part $3$). Now, if we consider the complex conjugate we have $\overline{(x+y\zeta_p^i) }\equiv  eta \zeta_p^{-k}a \pmod p$. Looking at $(x+y\zeta_p^i)-\zeta_p^{2k}\overline{(x+y\zeta_p^i) }$ then gives the result. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Each part separately: reduction mod $p$ with Fermat's little theorem, prime-ideal argument with $(1-\zeta_p)$, Frobenius congruence, basis comparison, and complex conjugation with the unit lemma.

nodes.name: Part 1
nodes.statement: Reducing modulo $p$, using Fermat's little theorem, you get that if $x \equiv y \equiv -z \pmod $, then $3z \equiv 0 \pmod p$. But since $p >3$ this means $p |z$ but this contradicts $\gcd(xyz,p)=1$. Now, if $x \equiv y \pmod p$ then $x \not \equiv -z \pmod p$ we can relabel $y,z$ so that wlog $x \not \equiv y$ (this uses that $p$ is odd).

nodes.name: Part 2
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{lemma: fac of p in p_th root} gives that $u$ is a unit. So all that needs to be proved is that the ideals are coprime. Assume not, then for some $i \neq j$ we have some prime ideal $\mathfrak{p}$ dividing by $(x+y\zeta_p^i)$ and $(x+y\zeta_p^j)$. It must then also divide their sum and their difference, so we must have $\mathfrak{p} | (1-\zeta_p)$ or $\mathfrak{p} | y$. Similarly, $\mathfrak{p}$ divides $\zeta_p^j(x+y\zeta_p^i)-\zeta_p^i(x+y\zeta_p^j)$ so $\mathfrak{p}$ divides $x$ or $(1-\zeta_p)$. We can't have $\mathfrak{p}$ dividing $x,y$ since they are coprime, therefore $\mathfrak{p} |(1-\zeta_p)$. But from lectures we know that since $(1-\zeta_p)$ has norm $p$ it must be a prime ideal, so $\mathfrak{p}=(1-\zeta_p)$. Now, note that $x+y \equiv x+y\zeta_+p^i \equiv 0 \mod \mathfrak{p}$. But since $x,y \in \mathbb{Z}$ this means we would have $x+y \equiv 0 \pmod p$, which implies $z^p \equiv 0 \pmod p$ which contradicts our assumptions.

nodes.name: Part 3
nodes.statement: This is easy. Just use $(x+y)^p \equiv x^p + y^p \pmod p$ and that $\zeta_p$ is a $p$-th root of unity.

nodes.name: Part 4

Now, as $\alpha/n \in \mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$, pick the basis of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$ which does not contain $\zeta_p$ (which is possible as any subset of $\{1,\zeta_p,\dots,\zeta_p^{p-1}\}$ with $p-1$ elements forms a basis of $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$.]). Then $\alpha=\sum_i b_i \zeta_p^i$ where $b_i \in \mathbb{Z}$. Therefore comparing coefficients, we get the result.

nodes.name: Part 5

Now, if we consider the complex conjugate we have $\overline{(x+y\zeta_p^i) }\equiv \beta \zeta_p^{-k}a \pmod p$. Looking at $(x+y\zeta_p^i)-\zeta_p^{2k}\overline{(x+y\zeta_p^i) }$ then gives the result.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 19
nodes.statement: First thing is to note that if $x^p+y^p=z^p$ then \[z^p=(x+y)(x+\zeta_py)\cdots(x+y\zeta_p^{p-1})\] as ideals. Then since we know the ideals are coprime, then by lemma \ref{lemma: ideals mult to power} we have that each $(x+y\zeta_p^i)=\mathfrak{a}^p$, for $\mathfrak{a}$ some ideal. Note that, $[\mathfrak{a}^p]=1$ in the class group. Now, since $p$ does not divide the size of the class group we have that $[\mathfrak{a}]=1$ in the class group, so its principal. So we have $x+y\zeta_p^i=u_i\alpha_i^p$ with $u_i$ a unit. So by \ref{theorem:FLT facts} part $5$ we have some $k$ such that $x+y\zeta_p-\zeta_p^{2k}x-\zeta_p^{2k-1} \equiv 0 \pmod p$. If $1,\zeta_p,\zeta_p^{2k},\zeta_p^{2k-1}$ are distinct, then \ref{theorem:FLT facts} part $4$ (which uses that $p>3$) says that $p$ divides $x,y$, contrary to our assumption. So they cannot be distinct, but checking each case leads to a contradiction, therefore there can not be any such solutions.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $z^p$ into coprime ideals, each a $p$-th power and principal by regularity. Then parts 5 and 4 of Theorem 18 force $p\mid x,y$ or a case check contradiction.

nodes.name: Factor as ideals
nodes.statement: First thing is to note that if $x^p+y^p=z^p$ then \[z^p=(x+y)(x+\zeta_py)\cdots(x+y\zeta_p^{p-1})\] as ideals.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $z^p$ over $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_p]$.

nodes.name: Each factor is a p-th power
nodes.statement: Then since we know the ideals are coprime, then by lemma \ref{lemma: ideals mult to power} we have that each $(x+y\zeta_p^i)=\mathfrak{a}^p$, for $\mathfrak{a}$ some ideal.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 17 on coprime ideals.

nodes.name: Principal by regularity
nodes.statement: Note that, $[\mathfrak{a}^p]=1$ in the class group. Now, since $p$ does not divide the size of the class group we have that $[\mathfrak{a}]=1$ in the class group, so its principal. So we have $x+y\zeta_p^i=u_i\alpha_i^p$ with $u_i$ a unit.
nodes.statement_short: $p\nmid h_K$ makes $\mathfrak{a}$ principal.

nodes.name: Congruence from part 5
nodes.statement: So by \ref{theorem:FLT facts} part $5$ we have some $k$ such that $x+y\zeta_p-\zeta_p^{2k}x-\zeta_p^{2k-1} \equiv 0 \pmod p$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 18(5) gives a congruence.

nodes.name: Distinct exponents case
nodes.statement: If $1,\zeta_p,\zeta_p^{2k},\zeta_p^{2k-1}$ are distinct, then \ref{theorem:FLT facts} part $4$ (which uses that $p>3$) says that $p$ divides $x,y$, contrary to our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: If distinct, part 4 gives $p\mid x,y$.

nodes.name: Remaining cases
nodes.statement: So they cannot be distinct, but checking each case leads to a contradiction, therefore there can not be any such solutions.
nodes.statement_short: Checking the coincident cases gives a contradiction.

nodes.name: Fermat's Last Theorem for regular primes
nodes.statement: Let $p \geq 5$ be an prime number, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$. Assume that $p$ does not divide the size of the class group $\mathrm{Cl}_K$. Then \[x^p+y^p=z^p\] has no solutions with $x,y,z \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $xyz \ne 0$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard (Samuel; Marcus; Washington, cited in the introduction)
assumptions: $p \geq 5$ be an prime number, $\zeta_p$ a $p$-th root of unity and $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$
that $p$ does not divide the size of the class group $\mathrm{Cl}_K$
conclusions: \[x^p+y^p=z^p\] has no solutions with $x,y,z \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $xyz \ne 0$
nodes.statement_short: Kummer: for a regular prime $p\ge5$, $x^p+y^p=z^p$ has no solutions in non-zero integers.
nodes.label: FLT regular case
